910.name: Indigenous Peoples of Grenada
910.description: The indigenous settlement of Grenada by Arawak and later Carib (Kalinago) peoples, who called the island 'Camerhogne.' The Caribs fiercely resisted European colonization for over 150 years after initial contact.

sub_clusters.name: Arawak Early Settlement
sub_clusters.description: Arawak peoples from South America settled Grenada, establishing agricultural communities growing cassava, maize, and other crops. They developed pottery traditions and trade networks connecting the southern Caribbean islands.

sub_clusters.name: Carib Dominance — Camerhogne
sub_clusters.description: Carib (Kalinago) peoples migrated from South America and displaced the Arawaks, establishing dominance over the island they called Camerhogne. Their warrior culture and fierce resistance made Grenada one of the hardest Caribbean islands for Europeans to colonize.
key_events: Caribs establish Grenada (Camerhogne) as a stronghold in the southern Lesser Antilles

920.name: European Contact and Carib Resistance
920.description: Columbus sighted Grenada in 1498 and named it 'Concepción,' but Carib resistance prevented European settlement for over 150 years. Multiple colonization attempts were repelled before the French finally established a foothold.

sub_clusters.name: Columbus Sighting and Failed Settlement Attempts
sub_clusters.description: Columbus sighted the island in 1498, naming it 'Concepción' (later changed to 'Granada' by Spanish sailors). An English attempt at colonization in 1609 was repelled by the Caribs, as was a French attempt in 1638.
key_events: Columbus sights Grenada during his third voyage 1498

sub_clusters.name: French Colonization Under Du Parquet
sub_clusters.description: Jacques Dyel du Parquet, Governor of Martinique, purchased Grenada from the French Compagnie des Îles de l'Amérique and established the first permanent European settlement in 1649. Initial coexistence with the Caribs quickly deteriorated into conflict, culminating in the legendary mass suicide of Carib warriors at a cliff now known as 'Leapers' Hill' (Morne des Sauteurs) in 1651.
key_events: Du Parquet establishes first French settlement 1649
Carib warriors leap to their deaths at Leapers' Hill (Morne des Sauteurs) rather than surrender 1651

930.name: French and British Colonial Era
930.description: Grenada's colonial period under French and then British rule, the development of sugar and later nutmeg plantations, the importation of enslaved Africans, and Fédon's Rebellion — the most significant slave-led uprising in Grenadian history.

sub_clusters.name: French Plantation Colony
sub_clusters.description: Under French rule, Grenada was developed into a sugar, indigo, and cotton plantation colony. Enslaved Africans were imported in large numbers to work the estates. French culture, Catholicism, and Creole language deeply influenced Grenadian society and persist to this day.

sub_clusters.name: British Takeover and Sugar-Nutmeg Economy
sub_clusters.description: Britain acquired Grenada through the Treaty of Paris (1763). The British expanded sugar production and introduced nutmeg cultivation, which would eventually earn Grenada its 'Spice Island' reputation. Nutmeg trees, introduced from the East Indies, thrived in Grenada's volcanic soil.
key_events: Treaty of Paris cedes Grenada to Britain 1763
Introduction of nutmeg cultivation to Grenada

sub_clusters.name: Fédon's Rebellion (1795–1796)
sub_clusters.description: Julien Fédon, a free colored planter inspired by the French and Haitian Revolutions, led a massive rebellion in March 1795. He captured much of the island, held British hostages (executing several including the Lieutenant Governor), and controlled the interior for over a year before being defeated. Fédon himself was never captured; his fate remains unknown.
key_events: Julien Fédon launches rebellion — March 2, 1795
Fédon captures most of Grenada and executes British hostages
British forces suppress rebellion 1796 — Fédon's fate remains unknown

940.name: Emancipation and the Rise of the Spice Island
940.description: The abolition of slavery, emancipation in 1834, and the transformation of Grenada's economy from sugar to spice production — particularly nutmeg, mace, and cocoa — which would define its economic identity.

sub_clusters.name: Emancipation and Labor Transition
sub_clusters.description: Emancipation in 1834 freed approximately 24,000 enslaved people. The apprenticeship period ended in 1838, and freed people moved into small-scale farming and the growing spice trade, reducing dependence on the sugar plantation system.
key_events: Emancipation of enslaved people in Grenada 1834
Apprenticeship system ends — full freedom achieved 1838

sub_clusters.name: Nutmeg and Cocoa Economy Development
sub_clusters.description: Sugar declined and Grenada transitioned to nutmeg, mace, cocoa, and other spices as primary exports. By the late 19th century, Grenada was one of the world's leading nutmeg producers, earning its enduring title as the 'Spice Island' — nutmeg even appears on the national flag.

950.name: Labour Movement and Independence
950.description: The emergence of labour organizing, the peculiar political career of Eric Gairy (including his famous interest in UFOs), and the achievement of independence on February 7, 1974.

sub_clusters.name: Eric Gairy and the Labour Movement
sub_clusters.description: Eric Gairy founded the Grenada United Labour Party (GULP) and organized agricultural workers, leading major strikes in 1951 that transformed Grenadian politics. Charismatic but increasingly erratic, Gairy championed workers' rights while developing authoritarian tendencies.
key_events: Gairy leads 1951 agricultural workers' strike — major concessions won
Gairy becomes Chief Minister 1961

sub_clusters.name: Independence and Gairy's UFO Politics
sub_clusters.description: Grenada gained associated statehood in 1967 and full independence on February 7, 1974, with Eric Gairy as first Prime Minister. Gairy became internationally known for his speeches at the United Nations about UFOs and unidentified flying objects, while domestically his 'Mongoose Gang' thugs intimidated opponents.
key_events: Independence of Grenada — February 7, 1974
Gairy addresses UN General Assembly about UFOs

950.name: The Grenadian Revolution and US Invasion
950.description: The New Jewel Movement's bloodless coup against Gairy, Maurice Bishop's revolutionary government, the internal power struggle and Bishop's murder, and the US military invasion of October 1983.

sub_clusters.name: Maurice Bishop and the New Jewel Movement
sub_clusters.description: On March 13, 1979, the New Jewel Movement (NJM) led by Maurice Bishop overthrew Eric Gairy in a bloodless coup while Gairy was abroad. Bishop established a People's Revolutionary Government, pursued socialist policies, expanded healthcare and education, and built close ties with Cuba and the Soviet Union. The Point Salines International Airport, built with Cuban assistance, became a point of contention with the United States.
key_events: NJM overthrows Gairy in bloodless coup — March 13, 1979
Bishop establishes People's Revolutionary Government

sub_clusters.name: US Invasion — Operation Urgent Fury (October 1983)
sub_clusters.description: An internal power struggle between Bishop and hardliner Bernard Coard led to Bishop's house arrest, a massive popular demonstration demanding his release, and ultimately the execution of Bishop and several supporters on October 19, 1983. Six days later, on October 25, the United States invaded Grenada ('Operation Urgent Fury') with approximately 7,600 troops, citing the need to protect American medical students and restore order.
key_events: Maurice Bishop executed by army faction — October 19, 1983
US invades Grenada (Operation Urgent Fury) — October 25, 1983
Approximately 7,600 US troops deployed to the island

sub_clusters.name: Post-Invasion Democratic Restoration
sub_clusters.description: After the US withdrawal, Grenada restored democratic governance with elections in 1984 won by Herbert Blaize's New National Party. The country rebuilt its institutions and economy, with tourism and spice exports as the primary economic drivers.

960.name: Contemporary Grenada
960.description: Modern Grenada confronting climate vulnerability, the devastating impact of Hurricane Ivan in 2004, economic recovery, and the continued importance of the spice trade and tourism.

sub_clusters.name: Hurricane Ivan Devastation — 2004
sub_clusters.description: Category 3 Hurricane Ivan struck Grenada on September 7, 2004, causing catastrophic damage. Approximately 90% of buildings were damaged or destroyed, the nutmeg crop was devastated (destroying an estimated 80% of nutmeg trees which take 7–10 years to mature), and the island's infrastructure was crippled.
key_events: Hurricane Ivan devastates Grenada — September 7, 2004
90% of buildings damaged or destroyed
80% of nutmeg crop destroyed — decade-long recovery for the Spice Island economy

sub_clusters.name: Economic Recovery and Diversification
sub_clusters.description: Grenada's long recovery from Hurricane Ivan, the replanting of nutmeg groves, development of tourism (particularly eco-tourism and the underwater sculpture park), and efforts to diversify beyond traditional agriculture and tourism.

sub_clusters.name: Climate Resilience and Spice Trade Revival
sub_clusters.description: Grenada's ongoing efforts to build climate resilience, revive the spice industry, and maintain its 'Spice Island' identity while adapting to increasingly severe weather patterns. The country remains the world's second-largest nutmeg producer after Indonesia.

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
